divide_policy.text:
Policy: split inputs into hint levels.

Level 1 — no_hints:
- Use only schema facts (tables, columns, types, keys, constraints, relationships).
- Do NOT include storage-plan hints, notes, optimization or implementation advice.

Level 2 — organization_level:
- Present organized schema facts using clear headings and groupings (Overview; Tables/Entities; Columns and Types; Keys and Constraints; Relationships).
- Still do NOT include storage-plan hints or notes.

Level 3 — all_hints:
- Include schema facts plus all hints and notes present in the storage plan.
- Do NOT invent new hints, storage decisions, indexes, layouts, encodings, or implementation details.
- If something is only implied by the storage plan, mark it as "Implied by storage plan".

For each level, also produce a short one-sentence data structure description for downstream code generation.

Return valid JSON only, in this shape, using exactly the level names declared below:
{"levels": {"<level_name>": "<level text>"}, "data_structure_descriptions": {"<level_name>": "<short data structure description>"}}

Declared level names: ${level_names}

expert_knowledge.text:
# Memory Access & Data Movement

1. Ensure sequential memory access patterns
Traverse memory linearly whenever possible. Seuquential access maximizes cache line utilization and hardware prefetch efficiency.

2. Prefer pointer iteration over indexed access in tight loops - ensure sequential memory access patterns
Sequential pointer traversal reduces address recomputation and improves auto-vectorization.

3. Prefetch data when accessing through indices
If you access arrays indirectly through an index list, the CPU cannot predict what memory will be needed next. Manually prefetching upcoming elements helps hide memory latency and reduces cache misses.

4. Copy small records into local variables
When repeatedly accessing multiple fields of a small struct, copy the struct into a local variable first. This allows the compiler to keep values in registers instead of reloading them from memory.

5. Avoid unnecessary move or copy operations
Use in-place construction and rely on compiler elision where possible.

# Loop Structure & Invariants

6. Hoist invariant work out of loops
Any computation, lookup, or reference that does not change per iteration must be moved outside the loop.

7. Eliminate repeated structural checks
Do not repeatedly verify conditions that are constant or guaranteed.
Compute once, cache once, or rely on established invariants.
Also, if different conditions require different processing strategies, determine the strategy before the loop starts and then run the appropriate version. Avoid checking the same conditions repeatedly while scanning data.

8. Decide execution strategy before entering the loop
If multiple processing modes exist, select the mode once and run a dedicated loop variant.

9. Avoid duplicating large loop bodies
If several branches run almost identical loops with only small differences in filtering, combine them into one loop and control behavior with flags. This keeps code smaller, improves instruction cache usage, and helps the compiler optimize better.

# Control Flow

10. Minimize branching in inner loops
Use early-continue filtering or direct predicate-based accumulation.
Avoid auxiliary state flags if results can be inferred.

11. Consider branchless computation when branch prediction is poor
If control flow is unpredictable, replace branches with arithmetic masking.
Computing a boolean condition and using it to control arithmetic (e.g., multiply by 0 or 1) can be faster than branching, especially in large scans.

# Arithmetic & Computation Cost

12. Remove expensive arithmetic from hot loops
Avoid division or other high-latency operations per element.
Precompute constants or perform normalization after aggregation.

13. Avoid expensive general-purpose parsing in hot paths
Do not use high-level string conversions or substring allocation inside tight loops (e.g. std::stoi, std::stod, substr).
Prefer fixed-format, allocation-free parsing directly from raw memory.

# Containers & Lookup Struktures

14. Pre-size output containers using realistic estimates
Estimate result size from selectivity or statistics to avoid dynamic growth.

15. Replace repeated linear searches with indexed lookup structures
Use hash-based or constant-time lookup instead of scanning collections repeatedly.

# Algorithm Selection

16. Use algorithms specialized for data characteristics
For fixed-width numeric keys or sortable primitives, prefer non-comparison-based or domain-specific algorithms.

# Compiler Optimization Signals

17. Communicate aliasing guarantees
Tell the compiler when memory regions do not overlap (e.g. restrict semantics).

18. Inline hot functions when beneficial
Reduces call overhead and exposes optimization opportunities.

# Vectorizaton & Hardware Utilization

19. Exploit SIMD parallelism where applicable
Process multiple elements per iteration using vectorized comparisons and masked arithmetic.

expert_knowledge_abstract_old.text:
An expert has given the following tips to consider when optimizing a custom in-memory OLAP database engine in C++. The workload is read-only and the set of queries is fixed.

• Prefer query-specific physical layouts over generic ones. Store only the columns used by the fixed queries, partition data along the primary filter dimension (often time), and cluster or sort data to match common predicates and group-by keys.

• Exploit the read-only nature of the data. Pre-join dimension tables into fact tables when joins are always the same, precompute frequently used expressions, and materialize partial or full aggregations that match the fixed query set.

• Use aggressive data skipping. Maintain per-partition or per-chunk min/max (zone maps) on filtered columns, dictionary-ID presence sets for equality predicates, and lightweight bitmaps where selectivity is high.

• Dictionary-encode all strings and low-cardinality columns. Execute predicates, joins, and group-bys on integer IDs instead of strings. Choose encodings per column and per partition to maximize compression and minimize memory bandwidth.

• Sort or cluster data intentionally to improve both compression and execution speed. Sorting by filter and group-by keys enables RLE, delta encoding, better cache locality, and faster aggregations.

• Eliminate general-purpose execution overhead. Build query-specific execution pipelines with no virtual dispatch, no iterator-style operators, and minimal branching. Hardcode predicate constants, join keys, and aggregation logic where possible.

• Use vectorized execution throughout. Process data in fixed-size batches, combine predicates into single kernels, and carry selection vectors or bitsets instead of materializing intermediate results.

• Leverage SIMD aggressively. Use SIMD comparisons for filters, SIMD hashing or probing where applicable, and branchless aggregation kernels to reduce misprediction and instruction overhead.

• Optimize joins for fixed schemas. Prefer perfect hashing or array-based joins when keys are dense. Otherwise, build dimension hash tables once and reuse them across queries. Radix-partition joins when hash tables exceed cache.

• Optimize aggregations for predictability. Use per-thread local aggregation with a merge phase. For dense or low-cardinality group keys, use direct indexing instead of hash tables.

• Pre-size and specialize hash tables. Avoid rehashing, store hash values alongside keys, and use open-addressing or cache-friendly probing schemes.

• Be NUMA-aware. Partition data by NUMA node, run scans locally, and replicate small read-only structures per node to avoid cross-socket traffic.

• Avoid dynamic memory allocation in hot paths. Use arena or region allocators with query-lifetime memory and eliminate malloc/free during execution.

• Avoid features that only benefit ad-hoc or mutable workloads. Skip cost-based optimizers, generic indexes, tuple-at-a-time execution, complex concurrency control, and transactional abstractions unless strictly required.

• Implement optimizations in a high-impact order: 
  1) columnar layout with partitioning and dictionary encoding
  2) data skipping and projection pruning
  3) clustering/sorting to match query patterns
  4) precomputation (joins, expressions, aggregations)
  5) vectorized and SIMD execution
  6) NUMA-aware parallelism and memory placement
  7) query-specific compiled execution pipelines

fix_compile_errors.text:
The code you generated has an issue. Fix it.

Compiler: ${compiler} with ${cpp_standard}
Command that failed:
${command}

Diagnostics or Verification Issue:
${diagnostics}

Rules for the fix:
- Fix the cause, not the symptom. Do not silence a diagnostic by deleting the code that triggers it, by casting the type away, or by widening a signature until it compiles.
- Do not change the input/output interface of the generated entry points.
- Do not weaken the storage layout to make a query compile. If a query genuinely cannot be expressed against the current layout, say so explicitly instead of quietly changing the layout.
- Keep the project buildable: if a fix requires a new include or a new declaration, add it.
- Change as little as possible. A large rewrite hides which edit actually fixed the error.

You have tools to read the current code by symbol and to recompile. Read the specific function or class named in each diagnostic before editing it — do not guess at the surrounding code. After editing, recompile and confirm the diagnostics are gone.

If a diagnostic is a warning rather than an error and the code is correct as written, leave it and say why.

COMMON ISSUES WITH OUTPUT FORMAT:
- If the comparison shows "row count differs", check your output delimiter. It MUST be a single comma ','.
  Never use pipes '|', spaces, or other characters.
- If parsing shows wrong column count, the delimiter in your code may be wrong.
- Strip trailing whitespace and control characters (including \r, \n) from string columns before output.

hppgen_policy.text:
Generate the storage-layout header for an in-memory, read-only analytical C++ query engine.

You are given one hint level: the schema facts, and — depending on the level — the storage-plan hints that accompany them. Implement exactly what the level text supports and nothing more.

The header must contain:

1. The column and table structures
   - One struct per table, holding its columns as contiguous containers.
   - Variable-length values as an offset array plus a character data array, not as a container of std::string per row, unless the level text says otherwise.
   - Nullability only for columns the schema marks nullable.
   - Fixed-width encodings where the level text calls for them (dictionary ids for low-cardinality strings, integral days for dates, narrowed integers).

2. The database structure
   - One struct aggregating every table, plus whatever lookup structures the level text describes.
   - Declare the ingestion entry point with exactly this signature: `${ingestion_signature}`. Its definition belongs in the loader, not here — declare it, do not define it, and do not change its name or signature.

3. Access-path members the level text justifies, and no others.

Hard rules:
- Everything goes in one self-contained header, wrapped in `#pragma once` and the namespace you are given.
- Header-only: declarations, type definitions and inline functions. No I/O, no Parquet reading, no query logic.
- Include only what you use, from the standard library.
- Compile cleanly under the project's C++ standard. Prefer std::vector and fixed-width integer types from <cstdint>.
- Do not invent tables, columns, indexes or encodings the level text does not support. If the level text omits something you would need, leave it out rather than guessing.
- Name types and members after the schema's own names so later stages can find them.

Output only the header source. No prose, no markdown fences.

optim_add_timings_collect_stats.text:
# Objective
Add comprehensive tracing instrumentation to measure query execution timing and row flow. The goal is to produce actionable data that identifies bottlenecks and validates optimizations.

# Requirements
## 1. Compilation & Overhead
- All profiling code must be behind #ifdef TRACE
- Zero overhead when compiled without the flag
- No allocations or I/O in hot paths—print results once at query end
- Use high-resolution timers (nanosecond precision)

## 2. Output Format
Stable, machine-parsable output with two line types:
```
PROFILE <section_name> <nanoseconds>
COUNT <counter_name> <value>
```
Names should reflect the specific query, and phase. E.g. `q1_titlescan_decode`, ...

## 3. Row Count Instrumentation
Track data flow through each operator:

Scan counters:
- rows_scanned - Total rows read
- rows_emitted - Rows passing filter (rows_scanned - rows_filtered_out)

Join counters:
- build_rows_in - Build side input rows
- probe_rows_in - Probe side input rows
- join_rows_emitted - Output rows

Aggregation counters:
- agg_rows_in - Input rows
- groups_created - Distinct groups
- agg_rows_emitted - Output rows (usually equals groups_created)

Sort counters:
- sort_rows_in
- sort_rows_out

General:
- query_output_rows - Final result count

## 4. Implementation Pattern
Use RAII-style scoped timers:
```
#ifdef TRACE
#define PROFILE_SCOPE(name) ScopedTimer _timer(name)
class ScopedTimer {
    const char* name;
    uint64_t start_ns;
public:
    ScopedTimer(const char* n) : name(n), start_ns(get_time_ns()) {}
    ~ScopedTimer() { record_timing(name, get_time_ns() - start_ns); }
};
#else
#define PROFILE_SCOPE(name)
#endif
```
Usage:
```
void execute_scan() {
    PROFILE_SCOPE("scan_total");
    {
        PROFILE_SCOPE("scan_decode");
        decode_data();
    }
    rows_scanned += n;
}
```

# YOUR TASK
Instrument the execution code of all queries to collect the tracing statistics. Use macros to add timing and counting instrumentation to all major operatorion (scan, join, aggregation, sort, etc.) and wherever you seem helpful according to the requirements above. Ensure that the output is stable and parsable, and that there is no overhead when TRACE is disabled.

optim_add_timings_collect_stats_per_quer.text: Add timing instrumentation to the execution code of the following queries: ${qids_str}. Verify your tracing implementation by using the RUN tool with tracing enabled (with scale factor ${sf}). Check that the output contains all required timing and counting information for these queries, and that the numbers make sense given the data size and query logic. If output is empty/null/0 where it shouldn't be, investigate and fix the instrumentation.${refer_to_prev}

optim_constraints.text:
Hard constraints (must obey):
- Leave the input/output interface unchanged.
- Single-threaded C++ only.
- Do not cheat by shifting work from execution to ingestion: No indexes, no materialized views, no pre-aggregation, no statistics collection used by execution, no query-result caching, no query-specific lookup tables or query-specific precomputed maps/arrays.
- Maintain ONE storage layout for all queries (no multiple copies of the same logical data).
- Storage layout must remain general enough that in theory arbitrary SQL could be executed.
- Always load all data from Parquet during ingestion (do not skip rows or columns).

optim_pretext_general.text:
You are an expert database engineer and skilled programmer.
Optimize a specialized high-performance database engine in C++ that is tailored to only execute a predefined set of queries. The queries to be supported are listed in `$queries_path` ($num_queries $query_str).

A basic implementation of the database engine is already done in your working directory.

optim_pretext_optim.text:
Your task is to optimize the existing codebase to achieve the best possible performance for the given queries.

During build, the database engine reads data from Arrow-Tables into a main-memory storage layout (in-memory database system).

You can modify any part of the existing codebase to improve performance, including data structures, ${storage_layout}algorithms, compression, and execution strategies. Focus on optimizing query execution times while maintaining correctness of the results. You can also change the ingestion pipeline if needed.

optim_w_expert_knowledge.text:
${constraints}

Optimize query ${query_id} using expert knowledge on high-performance in-memory OLAP systems.

An expert has given the following tips to consider when optimizing a custom in-memory OLAP database engine in C++. The workload is read-only and the set of queries is fixed:

${expert_knowledge}

Apply this tipps to bring down query runtime to ${target_rt} for sf ${sf} (current rt: ${current_rt}).

After making your changes, validate correctness and benchmark on scalefactor ${sf}. Make sure the performance improved. Otherwise, try again or remove your changes.

Be carefull with changes that affect other queries${bespoke_storage_related}. Avoid regressions on the other queries.

Turn off trace instrumentation in the run-tool for reliable benchmarking. Call run-tool with trace to gather updated statistics for bottleneck identification (will be written to `tracing_output.log`).

optim_w_human_reference.text:
${constraints}

Optimize query ${query_id} based on the collected tracing statistics in `tracing_output.log`.

Reduce the query runtime to less than ${target_rt} for sf ${sf} (current runtime: ${current_rt}). Approach this as Prof. Thomas Neumann or Matthias Jasny would: apply every low-level technique available, leave nothing on the table. Focus on the bottlenecks identified in the tracing output, but also reconsider the overall approach if the remaining gap is large.

Be carefull with changes that affect other queries${bespoke_storage_related}. Avoid regressions on the other queries.

After making your changes, validate that the query produces correct results and improved performance compared to the previous version. Benchmark on scalefactor ${sf}.
Make sure the performance improved. Otherwise, try again or remove your changes.

optim_w_trace.text:
${constraints}

Optimize the implementation of query ${query_id} based on the collected tracing statistics in `tracing_output.log`.

Focus on the code sections that are the bottlenecks according to the tracing output. After making your changes, validate that the query produces correct results and improved performance compared to the previous version. If performance did not improve, re-read the tracing statistics to re-identify bottlenecks and try again.

Target: reduce runtime to less than ${target_rt} for sf ${sf} (${factor}x improvement, current: ${current_rt}). Aim for even larger reductions where possible.

Be carefull with changes that affect other queries${bespoke_storage_related}. Avoid regressions on the other queries.

Turn off trace instrumentation in the run-tool for reliable benchmarking. Call run-tool with trace to gather updated statistics for bottleneck identification.
Make sure the performance improved. Otherwise, try again or remove your changes.

query_codegen_task.text:
Implement one SQL query as C++ against the generated storage layout.

You are given the query, the storage-layout header it must use, and the hint level's description of that layout. Produce a single self-contained translation unit that executes the query over data already loaded in memory.

Requirements:

1. Interface
   - Include the storage-layout header and use its types; do not redefine them.
   - Expose exactly one entry point: `${entry_signature}`.
   - Write results to the provided output stream, one row per line.
   - CRITICAL: Columns MUST be separated by a SINGLE CHARACTER: '${delimiter}' (comma).
   - Do NOT use pipes, spaces, or any other separator. Output format: column1,column2,column3
   - For string columns: trim all trailing whitespace, control characters, newlines and carriage returns before output.
   - Print numeric values so they compare equal to the reference output: integers without a decimal point, and DECIMAL columns with their declared scale.
   - ${header_rule}

2. Execution
   - Single-threaded. No SQL parsing at runtime: compile the query's plan into the code.
   - Choose join order and build sides from the cardinalities you were given, smaller side as the hash build side.
   - Respect the query's ORDER BY exactly; if it has none, emit rows in whatever order the plan produces.
   - Apply filters as early as possible and touch only the columns the query needs.

3. Constraints
   - Do not modify the storage layout, and do not add per-query indexes, materialized results or precomputed lookup tables. The layout is shared by every query.
   - Only the standard library. No external dependencies.
   - No undefined behaviour: check bounds where the plan does not already guarantee them, and initialize every accumulator.

Output only the C++ source for this one query. No prose, no markdown fences.

query_codegen_loader_task.text:
Implement the storage layout's ingestion entry point in C++.

You are given the storage-layout header this entry point must populate, and where the dataset lives. Produce a single self-contained translation unit that reads the dataset and builds the in-memory layout the header declares.

Requirements:

1. Interface
   - Include the storage-layout header and use its types; do not redefine them.
   - Expose exactly one entry point: `${entry_signature}`.
   - Populate every field exactly as the header's own comments describe: dictionary codes, dense ids, fixed-point scaled decimals, sorted permutations, zone maps, and any other encoding a column's comment documents. Those comments are the encoding specification, not a suggestion.

2. Reading the dataset
   - Read the dataset with the Apache Arrow / Parquet C++ API (`<arrow/...>`, `<parquet/...>`). One Parquet file per table, named after the table, under the dataset directory you are given.
   - Do not parse CSV, and do not invent a binary format of your own.

3. Constraints
   - Do not modify the storage layout, and do not add columns, tables or structures the header does not declare.
   - Standard library and Arrow/Parquet only. No other external dependencies.
   - No undefined behaviour: check bounds, and initialize every buffer you allocate.

Output only the C++ source for the loader. No prose, no markdown fences.

query_codegen_main_task.text:
Implement the engine's command-line entry point in C++.

You are given the storage-layout header, the dispatch declarations that route a query id to its implementation, and the exact command line this program must satisfy. Produce a single self-contained translation unit.

Requirements:

1. Interface
   - Include the storage-layout header and the dispatch header; use their declared types and functions, do not redefine them.
   - Parse argv so the program accepts exactly the command line given, in any argument order.
   - Build the database exactly once, by calling `${entry_signature}`, before dispatching any query.
   - Look up the requested query through the given dispatch function and call it with the database and the output destination the command line specifies.

2. Constraints
   - Do not implement any query logic here; this file only wires argument parsing, one-time ingestion and dispatch together.
   - Standard library only. No Arrow/Parquet includes here -- ingestion is the loader's job, not this file's.
   - Exit non-zero and report a clear message on a bad argument or an unknown query id.

Output only the C++ source for the entry point. No prose, no markdown fences.

storage_plan_policy.text:
You are an expert database engineer designing the in-memory storage layout for a read-only analytical query engine.

You are given a schema, a fixed set of queries, and optionally dataset statistics. Produce a storage plan: the concrete in-memory layout the engine should build after ingestion, justified by the query workload.

Cover each of the following:

1. Physical layout per table
   - Column-major, row-major, or hybrid, and why the workload favours it.
   - The concrete C++ representation for each column (contiguous arrays, offset+data pairs for variable-length values, bitmaps for nullability).
   - Fixed-width encodings where the schema permits them (dictionary encoding for low-cardinality strings, integer narrowing, date/time as integral days or micros).

2. Access paths
   - Which columns need sorted order, a hash index, or a zone map, and which queries justify each one.
   - Join keys that should be pre-resolved to dense integer ids at build time.
   - Group-by keys that should be dictionary-encoded so aggregation can use dense array slots instead of hashing strings.

3. Data movement
   - What is materialized once at build time versus recomputed per query.
   - Where sequential access is preserved, and which columns are co-located because they are read together.

4. Memory budget
   - An estimate of bytes per table given the statistics, if statistics were provided.
   - Any layout choice that trades memory for query time, stated explicitly as a trade.

Hard constraints:
- Every layout decision must be traceable to the schema or to a specific query. Do not invent columns, tables, indexes or workload characteristics that the inputs do not support.
- All data is loaded from Parquet during ingestion. Ingestion cost is acceptable; per-query cost is what matters.
- Assume single-threaded query execution unless the queries clearly require otherwise.
- If the statistics are absent, say which decisions are provisional on cardinality and what you assumed.

Write the plan as structured prose with headings, not as code. Downstream stages generate the C++ from it, so the plan must be precise enough to implement without further guessing, and must not contain the implementation itself.
